thread.title: You Can't Handle the Truth About User Data

author: Barron's
title: You Can't Handle the Truth About User Data

organizations.name: truth about user data bloomberg news tech

text:
Bloomberg News Tech's great data debate may be more complicated than it looks.
Facebook (ticker: FB) and Apple ( AAPL ) have traded barbs in recent weeks on their respective approaches toward the treatment of user data.
Apple Chief Executive Tim Cook last month again championed his company's strict privacy approach and took to task Facebook and other ad-dependent companies that aggressively monetize data. Last year, 98% of Facebook's revenue came from advertising; Apple has minimal, if any, ad exposure and it doesn't mention ad revenue in its risk section.
"We reject the excuse that getting the most out of technology means trading away your right to privacy," Cook said in a commencement speech at Duke University . "So we chose a different path, collecting as little of our data as possible, being thoughtful and respectful when it's in our care because we know it belongs to you."
Yet the debate doesn't appear as black-and-white as Cook has made it out to be, based on developing news stories in recent days.
Facebook reached data-sharing agreements with at least 60 device makers-including Apple, Amazon ( AMZN ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Samsung Electronics (South Korea: 005930), and BlackBerry ( BB )-over the last decade that gave them "deep" access to vast amounts of Facebook's users' personal information, according to a New York Times report on Sunday.
As Facebook grew in influence on those computing platforms, and device makers gained access to the data of those users and their friends without their explicit consent, it may have violated Facebook's privacy protections and compliance under a 2011 consent decree with the Federal Trade Commission .
"Sure looks like [Facebook CEO Mark] Zuckerberg lied to Congress about whether users have'complete control' over who sees our data on Facebook," Rep. David Cicilline [D., R.I.], who is a ranking member of the House Judiciary Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial, and Antitrust Law, said after the Times report. "This needs to be investigated and the people responsible need to be held accountable."
Facebook strongly disputed the report. "Contrary to claims by The New York Times , friends' information, like photos, was only accessible on devices when people made a decision to share their information with those friends," Ime Archibong , Facebook's vice president of product partnerships, said in a blog post .
Facebook has muted some of the partnerships since April, shortly after news reports in March that political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica gathered the private information of up to 87 million Facebook members without their permission, sparking howls of protest from lawmakers and regulators.
As for Cook's criticism of ad-driven business models, a report from The Wall Street Journal suggests that could be changing. On Friday, it reported Apple is looking into mobile advertising and has talked to Snap ( SNAP ) and Pinterest . The proposed "Apple network" would "distribute ads across their collective apps." Apple would share revenue with the apps displaying the ads "with the split varying from app to app," the Journal said.
Apple has had limited experience, and revenue, from advertising. Cook went so far as to call ads that follow consumers on the Internet "creepy" in an interview with MSNBC in April.
"The truth is we could make a ton of money if we monetized our customer," he said then. "If our customer was our product, we could make a ton of money."
Apple declined comment on the Journal report.
